title: WPW syndrome
subtitle: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
intro: This section is dedicated to my experience living with and treating Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome — a congenital heart anomaly featuring an extra electrical pathway that can cause sudden tachycardia episodes.

status.title: current status
status.outcomeDesc: August 12, using the CARTO-3 system. The main extra pathway was located and ablated.
status.remaining: awaiting discharge and final test results
status.remainingDesc: a second, weak pathway was left untouched — it runs right next to the normal AV node, so removing it was too risky. final conclusions will come after follow-up tests and discharge.

step1.title: diagnosis & symptoms
step1.desc: episodes of sudden tachycardia caused by an abnormal electrical pathway in the heart.

step2.title: radiofrequency ablation (RFA)
step2.desc: the first operation to ablate the extra conduction pathway was performed. temporary relief followed.

step3.title: suspected recurrence
step3.desc: symptoms began to return, resting heart rate often staying at 90–100 bpm. 24-hour Holter monitoring confirmed recurrence concerns.

step4.title: follow-up surgery
step4.desc: a second RFA was performed using the CARTO-3 system. both sides of the groin were explored, and one extra pathway was found and ablated.

step5.title: outcome
step5.desc: the second pathway was left alone: it sits right next to the normal conduction node, and removing it was too risky. per the surgeon, it's weak, only partially conducting, and rarely causes trouble. doctors also noted my baseline heart rate simply runs high — 150 bpm lying down isn't considered tachycardia for me. currently awaiting discharge and final test results.

attractions.q: Can I ride extreme amusement park rides?
attractions.a: No, if the syndrome is active or a recurrence is suspected. Sudden adrenaline surges and heavy G-forces can trigger a severe arrhythmia episode.

sports.a: Active sports like football (soccer) are strictly forbidden. Only calm, moderate swimming is allowed, ensuring your heart rate stays low.

caffeine.q: Can I drink coffee or energy drinks?
caffeine.a: Coffee and energy drinks are categorically forbidden. The caffeine, taurine, and other stimulants they contain are highly likely to trigger a tachycardia episode.

cure.q: How effective is the RFA procedure?
cure.a: The primary success rate of RFA is around 90–95%, but there is a 6–10% chance of pathway recurrence (see this scientific article on <anchor>PubMed</anchor>). In case of recurrence, a repeat ablation is required.

inherited.a: It is a congenital heart condition, meaning you are born with it. The extra pathway is present from birth, though symptoms may manifest at any age.

procedure.title: how the procedure works: personal follow-up RFA experience
procedure.intro: Radiofrequency catheter ablation (RFA) and electrophysiological study (EPS) are high-tech, catheter-based vascular interventions rather than open-heart surgery. My second procedure was done on August 12 using the CARTO-3 system. Here is how it went:

step1.title: 1. Access on both sides
step1.desc: First, a local anesthetic is injected into the groin area. Then, an introducer sheath — a flat plastic port about the size of a flat finger — is inserted into the femoral artery. This time both the left and right groin were used, with thin, flexible electrode catheters guided through each one directly to the heart.

step2.title: 2. EPS & 3D mapping with CARTO-3
step2.desc: The CARTO-3 system under the operating table acts like a GPS, tracking the catheter tips to build a detailed 3D map of the heart chambers on a monitor. It lets the doctors pinpoint exactly where the extra conduction pathways run.

step3.title: 3. One pathway found and ablated
step3.desc: Mapping the heart from both sides, the doctors found an extra pathway that could be safely removed and ablated ('sealed') it with high-frequency electrical current.

step4.title: 4. The second pathway was left alone
step4.desc: They found another pathway — per the surgeon, weak and only partially conducting, rarely causing problems. It runs right next to the heart's normal conduction (AV) node, so removing it was too risky — it could have damaged the node itself. They decided to leave it as is.

step5.title: 5. Drug-induced stimulation & the ablation itself
step5.desc: During the procedure I was given drugs to raise my blood pressure (likely isoproterenol) — they made me feel hot, which helps the doctors see the conduction pathway more clearly. The most painful part of the whole procedure is the ablation itself: an intense pain around the heart and neck. I was given an oxygen mask during it, and the staff noted I was handling it well.

step6.title: 6. Afterward
step6.desc: Huge respect to the whole medical team, especially the surgeon and the anesthesiologist. Afterward, while waiting to be taken out of the operating room, I just talked with the anesthesiologist about life. Now it's recovery — awaiting discharge and final test results.
